name: Dependency theory
summary: Dependency theory holds that the underdevelopment of poor countries is produced by their place in the world capitalist economy, not by a lack of modernisation. Trade, finance, technology and foreign investment transfer surplus from a dependent periphery to a dominant core, and the structure is reproduced inside the periphery through local elites allied with foreign capital. Its strands differ on the remedy: ECLA structuralists and Cardoso and Faletto favoured protectionist industrialisation and reform, while neo-Marxists such as Frank and Dos Santos looked to a break with the system and socialism. It is chiefly an analysis of development and says little on most other policy questions.

scope: Latin American dependency theory as the reference works and Schmidt's survey present it: the structuralist reformers (Prebisch, Cardoso and Faletto) and the neo-Marxist strand (Frank, Dos Santos), with Dos Santos's 1970 essay as the canonical primary text. It excludes world-systems analysis as a separate subject and Wallerstein's own programme, and the later Marxist, postcolonial or anti-imperialist movements that borrow its ideas.

aliases.name: dependency approach
aliases.quote: Dependency theory is a macro-level theoretical perspective concerned with questions of extreme disparities between modern nations. How do we account for such disparities (income, standard of living, etc.) between nations? The dependency theorists argue that the economic and political arrangements of the global capitalist economy are the root cause of such disparities. According to the dependency approach, and contrary to the neoliberal economics or modernization theory, being integrated into the global capitalist economy exacerbates the Third World nations' dependency

authors.quote: Frank (1967, 1969), an early proponent, established the premise for dependency theory
Dos Santos maintained that the balance of payments is manipulated
Few more eloquent defenders of the broad dependency perspective have emerged than Brazil's Cardoso

notes: Evidence is words only. Themes searched: economy and trade, aid and debt, tariffs and industrialisation, class and exploitation, state and elites, revolution and socialism, world order, ecology, society, technology. The sources are about development; they record nothing on liberty, family, religion, gender, race, ecology or most government questions, so those are null, and the strands' remedies (socialist planning versus state-led capitalist industrialisation) are not settled for the school as a whole. Frank's and Cardoso's books were not available in full text, so Frank's and Cardoso's positions rest on the reference accounts.
